A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ZipMoE, with matching methods, original experiments, and theoretical appendices. Text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. The relocated cache-planning algorithm and renumbered equations can be matched.

before.justification: v1 reports original compression and hardware measurements, inference benchmarks on three MoE models, and cache-management ablations in Figures 1–4 and 7–10.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds memory-pressure experiments, planning sensitivity tests, initialization measurements, and further system comparisons in Section 5.1 and Appendix E.

M1.justification: The bit-field compression pipeline, cache-affinity scheduler, hierarchical cache management, and Algorithms 1–4 are retained. Compressor APIs receive additional documentation, while adaptation to separate CPU/GPU memory is proposed as future work; neither establishes an implemented method change.

E1.justification: The ShareGPT workload, three MoE models, and two Jetson configurations remain unchanged. v2 extends tested operating scenarios to background memory pressure and deliberately mismatched planning inputs. It adds no dataset, language, application domain, or evaluated hardware family.

E2.justification: Appendix E.3 newly evaluates FineMoE against ZipMoE on Qwen1.5-MoE across 5–30 GB memory footprints, reporting TTFT and TPOT in Tables 5–6. FineMoE's underlying work was already cited in v1 but was not evaluated there. Existing main comparators are retained.

E3.justification: v2 adds controlled evaluation designs: background RAM consumption of 0, 20, 24, 28, and 32 GB; planning-distribution smoothing with alpha from 0 to 1; and end-to-end compressor comparisons across memory budgets. These substantially extend the controls supporting performance attribution and robustness. The 10 GB memory footprint and batch size 16 newly stated for the existing cache ablation are disclosures, not demonstrated setting changes.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained cache-policy ablation, v2 adds quantitative component-gain attribution, OS page-cache isolation, sensitivity to inaccurate popularity estimates, expert-activation trace analysis, and end-to-end compressor sensitivity. Tables 1–2, 4, and 7 and Figures 11–12 investigate several previously untested explanations and robustness questions.

E5.justification: Both versions retain Figure 9's average curves and shaded ranges between the top and bottom 10% values. v2 adds no repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or revised uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: Original benchmark outcomes are retained, while substantial new results appear in Tables 1–7. Table 2 reports 56.64% TTFT and 53.32% TPOT reductions versus MoE-Infinity under 32 GB background memory consumption. Table 4 reports 16.8% and 9.5% slowdowns at maximum planning perturbation. Initialization timings, FineMoE comparisons, and compressor-specific latencies are also newly reported.

T1.justification: Appendix E.2 adds the formal perturbation definition F_tilde = (1-alpha)F + alpha E(F) for the sensitivity experiment. The existing scheduling approximation bound, maximum-entropy theorem, and proofs in Appendices A–D remain unchanged; their other edits concern explanation, placement, and equation numbering.

C1.justification: The introduction strengthens novelty positioning from an efficient edge inference engine to the first system accelerating mobile and edge MoE inference through lossless compression. The central system contributions and abstract's headline latency and throughput claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation of the gains: approximately 76% is attributed to the core system and 24% to cache management, with cache planning described as providing a moderate additional benefit. It interprets page-cache support as opportunistic, explains robustness through stable popularity ranks, discusses FineMoE's edge limitations, and explicitly identifies Jetson-only evaluation and separate-memory adaptation as future work.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a code-access URL, documents compressor-extension APIs, and discloses the existing ablation's 10 GB memory footprint and batch size 16. Appendix E.1 adds initialization costs and less than 1 GB additional buffering overhead. The main implementation stack and hardware specifications are retained; repository contents were not inspected.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations on quantization, edge computing, and scheduling, including Fu et al. and scheduling work by Davies et al. and Maiti et al. It also introduces explicit first-system positioning. FineMoE was already cited, and several other reference changes update metadata rather than introduce different works.

P1.justification: The original narrative and method exposition largely remain intact. v2 corrects wording, clarifies passages in Appendix B, adds Discussion and Extended Results sections and acknowledgements, and moves Algorithm 4 alongside Appendix C. Author contribution and publication information are also updated.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual presentation with seven tables covering attribution, memory pressure, initialization, sensitivity, FineMoE, and compressors, plus Figures 11–12 showing memory-pressure contributions and activation distributions. Figures 1–10 are retained. Algorithm 4 is relocated, and the scheduling bound becomes a displayed, numbered equation.

improvement.justification: v1 acknowledged page-cache benefits without isolating their contribution and did not empirically test inaccurate planning estimates. v2 addresses these important evidential gaps through memory-pressure controls and sensitivity experiments, while clarifying component contributions and adding a relevant comparator, deployment costs, and code-access information. This substantially strengthens support for the central efficiency claim. Run-count and uncertainty-reporting gaps remain, and broader hardware applicability is still untested.
